claim: The script that the Alt attack flow draws is one the advisory says steals sensitive data.
quote: CISA received a related malicious Bash script for analysis from a trusted third party. The analyzed script, deployed on or around April 12,exploits CVE 2022-22960 and allows a Horizon user to escalate privileges and execute commands and scripts as a superuser (sudo). The Bashscript also allows the user to collect network information and additional information.
issue: The Alt flow's nodes (publishCaCert.hzn overwritten with fd86ald0.pem, TAR archive, C2 20.232.97.189) are the advisory's 'related' Victim 2 script, which it says collects information and archives passwords and master keys, but never says exfiltrates or steals. 'Developed for data exfiltration' is said of TA1's script at Victim 1 (PDF p. 3). The link rests on shared indicators (fd86ald0.pem, 20.232.97.189), an inference made in Marc's 2026-08-17 ruling, not on what the advisory says of this script.
fix_text: 'draws a script that the advisory says steals sensitive data' -> 'draws a script that the advisory relates to TA1's, which collected and exfiltrated sensitive data'

claim: The advisory says the TA1 script collected and exfiltrated sensitive data (the basis of 'so its attacker stole data').
quote: The script, which contained VMware Workspace ONE Access directory paths and file locations, was developed for data exfiltration [TA0010].The malicious script collected [TA0009] sensitive files–including user names, passwords, master keys, and firewall rules–and stored them in a“tar ball”
issue: Supports the conclusion for TA1's script, which shares the fd86ald0.pem indicator with the Alt flow's script (TA1 'deleted ... fd86ald0.pem', same page).

claim: Table C.1 row: the advisory is the threat report behind classifying CISA AA22-138B (Alt) as c1 (stole data, did not impede systems).
quote: The script overwrites the publishCaCert.hzn script on fd86ald0.pem file and executes commands that compress a list of files containinginformation such as network interface configuration, list of users, passwords, masterkeys, hosts, and domains to a TAR archive.
issue: The advisory describes the intrusion the flow draws, and it reports no impediment (the miner download at 194.31.98.141 is only 'attempted', PDF p. 4). 'Stole data' rests on tying the Victim 2 script to TA1's exfiltrating script (see U0945); the advisory states collection and archiving for this script, not theft. Row is consistent with App. C's statement that this flow was decided by us.

claim: Table C.1 row: the advisory supports classifying CISA AA22-138B (TA1) as c1 (stole data, did not impede systems).
quote: TA1 downloaded a malicious shell script, which they used to collect andexfiltrate sensitive data.
locator: PDF p. 3 (web page, unpaginated), summary of the third-party report
issue: Adversarial read: TA1 also 'deleted many files and logs', which is indicator removal, not impeding the victim's systems; no encryption, wiping or hijacking is reported for TA1. Holds.

claim: Table C.1 row: the advisory supports classifying CISA AA22-138B (TA2) as c4 (neither stole data nor impeded systems).
quote: TA2 interacted with the server (without automation or scripts) and installed multiple webshells and a reverse securesocket (SOCKS) proxy.
locator: PDF p. 3 (web page, unpaginated), summary of the third-party report
issue: Adversarial read: TA2's Unix commands 'enabled TA2 to view/etc/passwd and /etc/shadow password files ([TA0006], [T1003.008])' (PDF p. 4), credential access that an examiner could read as taking data; the advisory reports no exfiltration or impact for TA2, so 'neither' holds under the thesis's objective-level reading.
